name: Methoxydienone (Methoxy / 18-methyl)

lead: Methoxydienone is a 19-nortestosterone steroid synthesised in the 1960s and 70s during progestin research. It was never a medicine, and appeared later in online supplements.
No clinical studies have examined it in people.

paras: It is an anabolic-androgenic steroid and progestogen; animal-derived ratios reported on Wikipedia suggest anabolic activity when injected. Oral activity in humans has not been characterised.
No safety data in humans are published. A 2022 case report tied a supplement containing it to a detected 18-methyl steroid metabolite in a forensic urine sample, relevant for drug testing.

studies.title: Detection of 18-methyl steroids: Case report on a forensic urine sample and corresponding dietary supplements.

lead: Methoxydienone, also called methoxygonadiene, is a synthetic steroid of the 19-nortestosterone group, related to the progestin levonorgestrel. It was never marketed as a medicine but has been sold online as a 'designer steroid' supplement ingredient.[1][2]

It was synthesised by Herchel Smith and colleagues in the 1960s and 1970s during work on oral contraceptive progestins.[2] No human trials of it exist; the published literature on its use in people is a forensic case report.[1]

paras: Methoxydienone has a 17-ketone and, unlike many oral steroids, is not 17alpha-alkylated.[2] Wikipedia reports animal-derived anabolic-to-androgenic ratios of about 54:27 relative to testosterone propionate when injected, and states that no data exist on oral activity in humans.[2]

The compound came out of Herchel Smith's progestin research.[2] It later appeared as an ingredient in online supplements, which Rahnema and colleagues reviewed in 2015 among over-the-counter 'designer steroid' products.[2]

A 2022 forensic case report in Drug Testing and Analysis described a bodybuilder's urine sample containing a putative 18-methyl-19-nortestosterone metabolite. Supplements in the suspect's possession were found to contain methoxydienone, confirmed by mass spectrometry.[1]
